Despite the controversy, the BBC maintained Fury would remain on the list, citing that the decision was based on sporting achievement. The police force confirmed they had received complaints regarding his comments, which were being assessed for potential hate crime implications. While the GMP later clarified no specific crime had been recorded, the police inquiry underscored the seriousness with which his remarks were viewed.

Fury, who secured his world titles after defeating Wladimir Klitschko, has consistently maintained that his comments were taken out of context and that he is not a prejudiced individual, insisting he respects all people. Despite his defence, the ongoing controversy has cast a significant shadow over his boxing achievements and raised uncomfortable questions for the sport. The BBBofC meeting is anticipated to clarify whether Fury will face any disciplinary action, ranging from a reprimand to a fine or even a suspension, depending on the Board's assessment of his conduct and compliance with their code of ethics.

His pace in the opening stages clearly demonstrated his intent to build on the momentum gained from Mexico, where a last-gasp surge saw him snatch victory. The Tour de Course, often dubbed the 'Rally of 10,000 Corners', provides a stark contrast to the gravel and altitude of Mexico, demanding pinpoint accuracy and supreme confidence on high-speed tarmac. Meeke, driving his Citroen C3 WRC, seemed perfectly attuned to the demanding conditions, pushing hard from the very first kilometre. His ability to find an extra gear on the demanding Corsican roads left his rivals, especially championship leader Ogier, with little room for error. Ogier, ever the strategist, was playing a waiting game, conserving tyres and monitoring Meeke's incredible rhythm, knowing that any mistake on these narrow, tree-lined roads could be catastrophic. The centre, which conducts about 230 operations on children and 70 on adults each year, has the UK's largest ECMO unit (a form of partial cardiopulmonary bypass) which oxygenates blood of critically ill patients.
The unit will stop surgery for children but will remain open to diagnose patients and for monitoring and non-surgical treatment.

"That would lead to sustainable care for the future and also a big improvement in care."

He said travelling any further could be a real issue as Lewis recently suffered a cardiac arrest shortly after arriving at Glenfield.
Mr Fowlston said: "He could have had that cardiac arrest on the way to, say, Birmingham. Could he have had the same service in the back of an ambulance? I very much doubt it."

Officials said among those arrested is a commander of the Colombian left - wing rebel group , Farc . Police said the suspects were part of a transatlantic drugs ring run by the ' Ndrangheta a powerful organized crime syndicate based in Calabria, southern Italy. This operation highlights the growing partnership between Colombian drug producers, particularly remnant factions associated with the dissolved Farc insurgency, and the sophisticated distribution networks of European mafias. Investigators revealed that the cocaine shipments originated in remote jungle labs in Colombia, often in areas previously controlled by the Farc, who either directly cultivated coca or levied 'taxes' on independent producers for safe passage and processing.

The sailing boats were chosen for their ability to blend in with legitimate maritime traffic, making them less conspicuous than large cargo vessels, and for their capacity to carry substantial loads without attracting undue attention. The routes typically involved crossing the Atlantic, often utilizing strategically located island nations as re-provisioning points before reaching European ports, predominantly in Spain and Portugal, for onward distribution across the continent. This particular bust involved meticulous intelligence gathering over several years, a collaborative effort spanning multiple law enforcement agencies.

A significant breakthrough came with intelligence shared by The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), which had been tracking the cartel's activities and its nexus with various Colombian narco-trafficking groups. Authorities in Colombia and Italy, alongside Europol and other European police forces, executed synchronized raids following the DEA's lead. Among the arrests were key logistical managers in Europe and several suppliers in South America. The Farc commander arrested in Colombia was reportedly a crucial link, responsible for ensuring the quality and quantity of the cocaine supplied and facilitating its transport to coastal rendezvous points. Further investigations are underway in the region, including in areas near Santa Fe, where some of the preliminary processing and logistics for the illicit drug trade are suspected to have taken place, demonstrating the intricate web of this criminal enterprise. West Yorkshire Police confirmed last month that 16,000 tickets issued by police community support officers ( PCSO ) were not valid due because of an " administrative error " . But , the force said there was " no basis in law " for refunds , which would have " come from the public purse " . Many of the drivers paid the fines, unaware of the underlying error. The revelation sparked considerable public outcry and anger among those affected, who felt unfairly penalised by the West Yorkshire Police. Drivers expressed frustration that the force was acknowledging the invalidity of the tickets while simultaneously refusing any form of recompense. Legal experts weighed in, questioning the ethical implications of retaining funds collected unlawfully, even if there was no direct legal precedent for a refund. Some argued that while the law might not explicitly mandate refunds in such a unique administrative error scenario, the principle of unjust enrichment should apply, where one party should not benefit from another's loss caused by their own mistake.

The situation put the West Yorkshire Police under significant pressure to explain why such a fundamental error occurred and why transparency about the issue took so long. Critics pointed out that the public's trust in the police, particularly in the impartiality and correctness of their enforcement actions, could be severely damaged. The Police and Crime Commissioner for West Yorkshire acknowledged the serious nature of the administrative error and stated that a full internal review was underway to understand how the invalid tickets were issued by PCSOs for such an extended period without detection. This review aimed to identify weaknesses in the internal processes and implement robust measures to prevent a recurrence.

For the many individuals who had already paid their tickets, often under the threat of further penalties or points on their license, the news was a bitter pill. Some indicated they would explore avenues for collective legal action, seeking advice on whether a class-action lawsuit could compel the force to refund the monies. Consumer rights groups also got involved, advocating on behalf of the affected drivers and calling for a clearer legal framework to address situations where administrative errors by public bodies lead to financial detriment for citizens. The incident highlighted a significant loophole in the system, where a clear administrative blunder by the West Yorkshire Police left thousands of citizens out of pocket with seemingly no recourse, raising fundamental questions about accountability and citizen protection when dealing with official enforcement. The cost of individual legal challenges for the drivers would likely outweigh the value of the tickets, further complicating their options. The PCSO role and the scope of their powers were also re-examined in light of the incident.

Four men deny attempting to smuggle 35 people into Tilbury Docks , Essex . One man died in the container . Basildon Crown Court heard one defendant been caught in France with migrants in the back of his lorry 11 days before the Tilbury incident . Timothy Murphy from Londonderry was fined √Ç¬£5,000 in August . Prosecutor Michael Goodwin told the court that the 35 migrants, including 15 children, were discovered on August 16 last year inside a container on the MV Titania, which had arrived at Tilbury Docks from Zeebrugge, Belgium. Conditions within the sealed container were described as “inhumane and life-threatening,” with temperatures soaring and oxygen levels depleting rapidly during the 10-hour voyage. The court heard that the victims had been deliberately locked inside the unit.

Mr. Goodwin explained that port officials heard unusual noises coming from within the container. Upon opening it, they found terrified and struggling individuals, many suffering from severe dehydration and hyperthermia. Among them was Meet Singh, 47, from Afghanistan, who tragically died during the journey. A post-mortem examination concluded that his death was caused by a combination of dehydration and hyperthermia.

The prosecution alleges that the four defendants, Stephen McLaughlin, 31; Martin McGlinchey, 49; Christopher Murphy, 20; and Timothy Murphy, 33, all from Londonderry, were part of an organised criminal conspiracy to smuggle people into the UK for financial gain. Mr. Goodwin highlighted Timothy Murphy's previous conviction in France, where he was caught attempting to transport 15 migrants in his lorry. This incident, just days before the Tilbury tragedy, suggested a sophisticated and repeated enterprise.

The court heard evidence that the defendants had been in regular contact via burner phones, coordinating their movements leading up to the incident. CCTV footage and phone data linked them to the vehicle carrying the container and to locations near Zeebrugge. The prosecution argued that the defendants were fully aware of the dangerous conditions the migrants would endure and showed a callous disregard for human life.

All four defendants deny a charge of conspiracy to facilitate illegal entry into the UK and a charge of manslaughter in relation to Mr. Singh’s death. The trial at Basildon Crown Court is expected to last several weeks, with further evidence to be presented regarding the planning and execution of the smuggling operation and the role each defendant played. The focus remains on establishing the extent of their knowledge and involvement in this tragic event, which ultimately cost a man his life and put dozens of others in extreme peril at Tilbury Docks in Essex.

The Ministry of Justice ( MoJ ) said Ms Lennon was not dismissed for being a whistleblower . ' The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) maintained that Ms Lennon’s dismissal was the result of a comprehensive internal disciplinary process, unconnected to her claims regarding prison conditions. A spokesperson for the MoJ stated that all prison staff are expected to adhere to the highest standards, and where these are not met, disciplinary action will be taken. Citing employee confidentiality, they would not discuss specific details of Ms Lennon's case, but reaffirmed the decision followed a thorough investigation into her conduct, concluding that her actions constituted serious breaches of policy.

Kim Lennon, however, strongly refuted the MoJ’s narrative, asserting that the disciplinary charges against her were a deliberate attempt to discredit her and suppress vital information about the critical state of Lewes Prison. She told reporters that her complaints, made over an extended period, had consistently been met with insufficient action by management. "I reported serious instances of drug dealing, violence, and a complete lack of control, which put both staff and inmates at immense risk," Ms Lennon stated. "Instead of addressing these grave issues, the prison management chose to target me. They wanted to silence anyone brave enough to speak the truth about a system that is failing drastically." She highlighted that the current measures by the Ministry of Justice were clearly insufficient to tackle the deep-rooted problems within the prison.

Ms Lennon’s case brings to light the ongoing challenges faced by the MoJ in managing the escalating problem of drug smuggling and violence within the UK's prison estate. Independent oversight bodies and parliamentary committees have repeatedly raised concerns about the scale of the issue, with reports frequently citing staff shortages, overcrowding, and a lack of resources as contributing factors. Critics argue that the government's response to these systemic failures has been inadequate, leaving frontline officers like Kim Lennon vulnerable when they attempt to expose dangerous realities.

The former officer intends to take her case to an employment tribunal, where she hopes to present evidence not only of wrongful dismissal but also of the dire conditions she witnessed. "My appeal isn't just about my job; it's about exposing the truth for the safety of everyone inside those walls," said Ms Lennon, vowing to continue her fight regardless of the personal cost. She remains steadfast in her belief that the public has a right to know the true state of affairs within their prisons, and that the MoJ must be held accountable for its duty of care. Her legal team is currently preparing the documentation, confident that they can demonstrate that Ms Lennon was unfairly targeted for her whistleblowing activities. His century, a testament to his resilience and growing maturity, included 18 fours and two sixes, played across more than five hours at the crease. The early scares, being dropped and almost run out, only seemed to steel his resolve, as he focused on building a substantial total for his team. His dismissal by Andrew Salter, a rare lapse in concentration, came from a ball that spun sharply back into him, ending a truly memorable individual performance.

Glamorgan, despite their earlier breakthroughs, found it difficult to dislodge Pettini, whose experience shone through. Lukas Carey, though expensive in patches, continued to pose a threat with his pace and bounce, while Andrew Salter tried to tie down the scoring with his accurate left-arm spin. The two tracks, 'Shape of You' and 'Castle on the Hill', showcase different facets of Sheeran's musical artistry. 'Shape of You' is a catchy, rhythmic pop offering with a subtle dance influence, while 'Castle on the Hill' is a nostalgic, anthemic ode to his upbringing in Framlingham, Suffolk, capturing the essence of small-town life and youthful friendships. The contrasting styles demonstrate his versatility and broad appeal, ensuring both critical acclaim and commercial success. The immediate impact of both songs highlights the power of a well-executed comeback.

This phenomenal achievement comes amidst a highly competitive music landscape. While other artists like Drake have consistently dominated the charts in recent years with their own string of hits, Sheeran's simultaneous one-two punch is a unique feat that underscores his singular talent and dedicated fanbase. His return has undoubtedly revitalised the UK charts, bringing a fresh wave of excitement and setting a new benchmark for chart performance.

"It's been a long time coming," he remarked, referring to the creative process during his sabbatical. The Official Charts Company added that the sheer volume of streams and downloads for both tracks was staggering, easily surpassing all other entries. This unparalleled success solidifies Sheeran's position as one of the most influential and popular musicians of his generation, proving that a hiatus can sometimes be the perfect catalyst for even greater triumphs. His ability to connect with listeners on such an intimate level, coupled with his undeniable songwriting prowess, continues to set him apart in the global music scene. Fans eagerly await further announcements regarding his forthcoming album, which is now poised to become one of the biggest releases of the year. Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation have spoken of the risks of moving patients hundreds of miles . The warning comes as the results of a serious case review into the abuse of patients at the private hospital near Bristol are due to be released . The abuse was uncovered during secret filming by the BBC Panorama programme . Eleven people have admitted charges of ill - treatment and neglect related to the abuse . South Gloucestershire Safeguarding Adults Board ( SAB ) commissioned the review , carried out by an independent investigator. The review meticulously examined the systemic failures allowing horrific abuse at Winterbourne View, the private hospital near Bristol. It delved into circumstances leading to patients being placed far from families and communities, a key concern highlighted by Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation. Their long-standing campaigns consistently warned against inherent risks of distant placements, which isolate vulnerable individuals, hinder family visits, and create environments where neglect and abuse are less likely to be detected.

The serious case review, commissioned by the SAB, sought to identify not only direct perpetrators but also broader institutional and commissioning failures. It scrutinised oversight mechanisms, or lack thereof, from local authorities and NHS trusts responsible for patient placement at Winterbourne View. Findings are expected to be stark, revealing how a system designed to protect vulnerable adults failed them catastrophically. The BBC Panorama exposé, using secret filming to uncover shocking abuse, served as a crucial catalyst, forcing a national reckoning with care quality for people with learning disabilities and challenging behaviour in residential settings.

The eleven individuals who admitted charges related to ill-treatment and neglect represent a tragic failure of individual responsibility, but the review's scope goes far beyond individual culpability. It aims to provide recommendations to prevent such atrocities. These are anticipated to include a significant shift away from large institutional placements towards smaller, community-based care closer to homes and families. Strong calls are likely for improved regulation, robust inspection regimes, and enhanced staff training. Furthermore, the review is expected to highlight the critical need for better communication between care providers, commissioning bodies, and families, ensuring concerns are heard and acted upon promptly.

Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation have advocated for comprehensive reform, pushing for person-centred care prioritizing individual rights, dignity, and access to a full life within their community. Their warnings about perils of out-of-area placements, often driven by lack of appropriate local provision or cost-saving, have been tragically vindicated by Winterbourne View. The SAB's commitment to releasing the full findings of this independent review demonstrates a crucial step towards transparency and accountability. Lessons from this harrowing episode must drive genuine, lasting change across health and social care sectors, ensuring safeguarding of vulnerable adults remains paramount. The imperative is to learn from systemic failures and implement robust measures to protect those who rely on specialist care, preventing any recurrence of neglect and abuse. The review's findings will undoubtedly inform national policy and practice, reinforcing the urgent need for a fundamental shift in how care is commissioned and delivered for individuals with complex needs, moving from isolated institutional settings towards inclusive, community-based support.

The transition comes at a pivotal time for the Redmond-based software giant as it strives to redefine itself beyond its traditional Windows and Office strongholds.

This "devices and services" push, championed by Steve Ballmer, represents a fundamental shift for Microsoft. It aims to integrate hardware and software more seamlessly, mirroring the successful strategies of competitors like Apple. However, the pivot has not been without its challenges. The reception to Windows 8, Microsoft's flagship operating system designed for touch-enabled devices, has been mixed since its launch, failing to significantly boost PC sales in a declining market. The acquisition of Nokia's devices and services division, a deal spearheaded by Mr Ballmer, is central to this strategy, promising Microsoft greater control over its smartphone ecosystem and a stronger competitive position in the mobile space. Analysts believe that the success of this transformation will largely depend on the new leadership's ability to execute on Ballmer's vision while also adapting to rapidly evolving consumer demands.

The promised "wide range" of new products likely includes further iterations of the Surface tablet, potentially a smaller version, and new smartphones under the Nokia brand. The next generation Xbox console, though already launched, will also continue to be a key revenue driver. Despite the positive earnings, some analysts remain cautious, highlighting the intense competition in both the enterprise and consumer markets. The departing Mr Ballmer leaves behind a company in the midst of a massive strategic overhaul, and the next CEO will face the immense task of accelerating this transformation while simultaneously rekindling investor confidence and innovating at a pace previously unseen at Microsoft. The coming quarters will be critical in determining whether Microsoft can truly shed its legacy image and emerge as a dominant force in the mobile-first, cloud-first world.

The life - size bronze effigy of the Native American stands in Gravesend , Kent , where she died on her journey home to Virginia in 1617 . Historic England has renewed its Grade II listed status and updated details of her life and role in Transatlantic history , confirming the monument's significance in commemorating Pocahontas, known also as Matoaka. The statue, erected in 1958, serves as a poignant reminder of her brief but impactful time in England, where she was presented to King James I and Queen Anne. Her story embodies the early, complex interactions between European settlers and Native American communities, particularly her marriage to English tobacco planter John Rolfe, which was instrumental in a period of peace for the early Jamestown colony.

The updated Historic England listing now explicitly acknowledges her Algonquian heritage and the often-misrepresented narratives surrounding her life, highlighting the agency she exercised within challenging circumstances. This recognition underscores the effigy's importance not merely as a local landmark in Gravesend, Kent, but as a national symbol of a pivotal moment in global history. The Grade II listing ensures the continued preservation of this unique memorial, reflecting its special architectural and historical interest. It emphasizes her tragic death at a young age in Gravesend before she could return to her native Virginia, underscoring the profound human cost of early colonial expansion and intercultural exchange. The statue, therefore, invites contemplation on themes of cultural encounter, diplomacy, and the lasting legacy of those who bridged vastly different worlds.

They claim to have beaten the world distance and duration records by flying for more than 137 hours and travelling more than 5,209 miles ( 8,383 km ) . To set the records the team needed to beat the existing records by 1 % . " The Two Eagles balloon team is pleased to report the Two Eagles balloon has landed safely just off the Baja coast near La Paz, Mexico, after an epic journey across the Pacific Ocean. The successful splashdown concluded a historic flight that spanned over five days, shattering previous records for both duration and distance in a gas balloon. The team, led by American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev, had originally aimed for a landing in North America, possibly as far east as Kansas, but prevailing winds shifted their trajectory southward. Despite not reaching their initial optimal landing zone, the sheer scale of their achievement is undeniable.

The Two Eagles Balloon team confirmed the successful landing via satellite communication and social media updates, stating that both pilots were in good spirits and uninjured. Recovery efforts were immediately initiated by support vessels dispatched to their landing coordinates. This monumental flight, which began on Saturday from Saga, Japan, pushed the boundaries of manned ballooning. Their claimed duration of more than 137 hours surpasses the previous record of 137 hours, 5 minutes, 50 seconds set by the Double Eagle II in 1978. Similarly, the claimed distance of over 5,209 miles far exceeds the existing record for a manned balloon.

For official recognition by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI), the world's air sports governing body, the Two Eagles team needed to beat the standing records by at least 1%. Based on their preliminary data, they appear to have comfortably achieved this margin for both categories. The flight path of the Eagles took them across vast expanses of the Pacific, demonstrating remarkable resilience and navigational skill from Bradley and Tiukhtyaev. The two aviators endured extreme cold, turbulent weather, and the inherent challenges of prolonged flight at high altitudes within the confines of their gondola.

Their successful completion marks a significant milestone in ballooning history, validating years of planning, preparation, and technological innovation by the Two Eagles Balloon team. While awaiting official certification of their records, the mood among the team and supporters is one of immense elation and pride. This extraordinary journey not only sets new benchmarks but also inspires future generations of adventurers and aerospace engineers. The precision landing off the coast of Baja, though not the specific target, ensured the safety of the crew and the preservation of crucial flight data for record verification. It was a testament to the skill and endurance of American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev, who have etched their names into the annals of aviation.

He openly stated his belief that the school's actions were driven by discrimination and Islamophobia, prompting his decision to remove all his children from the local school system. In the UK , concern had risen sharply about the availability of talent . The number of chief executives concerned about the availability of key skills had risen sharply. This growing talent crunch in the UK, as revealed by the PwC survey, is seen as a significant threat to growth and competitiveness. Many UK businesses report struggling to find and retain staff with essential digital and technical competencies, leading to increased investment in upskilling existing workforces and a focus on attracting international talent where possible.

In contrast to the UK's talent focus, business leaders in Germany and France voiced different primary concerns. German CEOs, while relatively more optimistic than their French counterparts, were predominantly worried about global demand slowdowns and geopolitical instability impacting their export-heavy industries. The eurozone's tepid recovery also cast a shadow, with concerns over deflation and consumer spending remaining high. In France, chief executives were more preoccupied with domestic regulatory burdens and the need for structural reforms to stimulate economic activity. Confidence levels remained subdued across both nations, reflecting a cautious European outlook amidst ongoing economic uncertainties and the lingering effects of the debt crisis.

Globally, the PwC survey of over 1,300 CEOs highlighted a universal shift towards caution. Beyond Russia's unique challenges stemming from sanctions and falling oil prices, and the UK's specific talent woes, the overall sentiment was one of strategic retrenchment. Only 37% of chief executives globally expected economic improvement, down from 44%. This marked decline underscores a pervasive sense of uncertainty across various regions, influenced by factors ranging from commodity price volatility to geopolitical tensions. CEOs indicated a greater focus on operational efficiency, cost control, and organic growth strategies, with less appetite for aggressive expansion. Ms Jones emphasised Dr Croy's expert opinion, arguing Mr Capp suffered from an abnormality of mental functioning which substantially impaired his ability to understand his conduct, form rational judgment, or exercise self-control. Yemeni reports say the victims included the daughter of Anwar al - Awlaki , a militant killed by a US strike in 2011 . The raid was the first such operation authorised by President Donald Trump . The US military had previously said a Navy Seal , William " Ryan " Owens , 36 , died and three others were wounded. The Pentagon asserted the operation targeted al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) and yielded significant intelligence, calling it a successful mission. However, these claims were swiftly countered by Yemeni officials and human rights organizations, who reported a much higher civilian death toll and questioned the mission's efficacy and planning.

Reprieve, a UK-based human rights group, stated that its ground investigators confirmed the deaths of at least 23 civilians, including 10 children, in the Yakla raid. Among the child victims was eight-year-old Nawar al-Awlaki, daughter of the American-Yemeni cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, who was himself killed in a US drone strike in 2011. Her family confirmed her death, sparking further outrage and highlighting the complex human cost of counter-terrorism operations in Yemen. Local reports indicated widespread destruction, with houses damaged and several civilians caught in the crossfire.

The high civilian casualty count and the death of a US serviceman immediately put the raid under intense scrutiny, particularly as it was the first authorized military action of President Trump's administration. Critics, including some US lawmakers, raised concerns about the intelligence used to approve the mission and its execution. Senator John McCain, then chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, initially described the mission as a "failure" due to the loss of life, though he later softened his stance. The US military launched an investigation into the civilian casualties amidst persistent questions about the tactical success and strategic implications of the operation in Yakla, al-Bayda province.

From Winston Churchill's infamous visit to Belfast in 1912 to a 1963 Viking invasion re-enactment in a County Down fishing town, as well as tales of tourism, industrial heritage and sport, a dazzling mosaic of Ulster life is pieced together in unseen archive footage.
Hundreds of unique films have been released to the public to view online for free after the British Film Institute (BFI) unlocked its archive as part of a major history project, From Britain On Film.
Royal visits and Lord Mayor's shows are documented in the collection, as is the tale of Churchill's appearance in Belfast when he addressed an audience of nationalists in Celtic Park and gave his support to Home Rule.
There are also dozens of travelogues that were used to sell Northern Ireland to tourists in Great Britain and the United States, helping to boost tourism in the years before the Troubles.
And in sport, the 1930 Ulster Tourist Trophy race held at the Ards circuit in County Down is captured on camera. The event attracted thousands of spectators and commanded the attention of the motorsport world.
The real gems, however, are found in the footage of ordinary people doing extraordinary things.
Films of people at work in the spinning mills and constructing the M1 at Stockman's Lane in Belfast shows Northern Ireland's industry at its booming best.
Another film captures the first time Northern Ireland hosted the World Ploughing Championships, and fittingly it is a local man who takes the title.
The colour footage from the 1959 competition in Armoy, County Antrim, shows Lawrence McMillan's crowning moment as he gets his hands on the Golden Plough.
But perhaps most revealing of all is a 1938 recording of the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast.
It gives a rare glimpse into the casualty department and operating theatres as they were then, 10 years before the foundation of the National Health Service.
While medicine has advanced considerably in the eight decades since then, some aspects of healthcare in Northern Ireland appear to remain unchanged - the film ends with an appeal from the chairman of the hospital's management board to reduce waiting lists.
Francis Jones, of Northern Ireland Screen, which gathered much of the footage, said the aim of the project was to preserve delicate film that could otherwise be lost.
"There is a pure nostalgia value to film. It's different to reading a textbook or history book," he added.
"To actually see the film has that kind of visceral appeal and really strikes a chord with people."
The full From Britain On Film archive can be viewed at the BFI Player.

Rehtaeh Parsons, 17, of Nova Scotia, killed herself in April after being taunted over a photo of her alleged rape by four boys, her mother has said.
Two 18-year-old men were arrested on Thursday in connection with the photograph.
The men, who have not been named, will be prosecuted in a juvenile court.
"We hope that today's arrests help the community to heal," Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Chief Superintendent Roland Wells of the Halifax district said in a statement on Thursday evening.
"A young girl has died in what was a tragic set of circumstances. We all need to reflect on how we as a community can come together in Rehtaeh's memory and see what we can do to work together to support our youth."
One of the men was charged with two counts of distribution of child pornography, the other with one count each of making child pornography and distribution of child pornography.
The RCMP said the names of the accused would not be released because they were youths at the time of the alleged offence, and warned Halifax residents who believe they know the identities of the accused not to release them on penalty of prosecution, nor to take vigilante action.
According to Rehtaeh's mother Leah Parsons, the Nova Scotia teen went to a party in 2011, when she was 15, and became inebriated after drinking vodka.
The girl told her parents that while she was heavily intoxicated, she was raped by four boys, and someone took a photograph of it.
The photograph was circulated online, and soon her schoolmates began taunting her over the photograph. The bullying was incessant, her mother said.
"She was never left alone," Ms Parsons told CBC News in April after Rehtaeh's suicide.
"Her friends turned against her, people harassed her, boys she didn't know started texting her and Facebooking asking her to have sex with them since she had had sex with their friends. It just never stopped."
Rehtaeh died in April in hospital, several days after attempting suicide.

Logan Murdoch suffered serious injuries in the crash and was not breathing when the Great North Air Ambulance team arrived . Hayley Murdoch , 29 , and Sheila Dixon , 71 , both from Carlisle , died following the collision at Newby Cross in 2016 . Dr Laura Duffy called Logan , years after that harrowing day, to marvel at his incredible journey back to health. She vividly recalled the scene at Newby Cross, describing it as one of the most challenging she had ever encountered. Logan had been clinically dead, but through the swift, coordinated efforts of the emergency services – the first responders, paramedics, and the air ambulance crew – he was resuscitated at the roadside. He was then airlifted to the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle in a critical condition, placed in an induced coma, and remained there for several weeks, fighting for his life. His family, already reeling from the devastating loss of Hayley Murdoch and Sheila Dixon, braced themselves for the worst, enduring agonizing days and nights by his bedside.

Against all odds, Logan began a slow, arduous recovery. Dr Duffy recounted the initial prognosis, which had been bleak, suggesting severe brain damage and long-term disability were highly probable. Yet, Logan’s resilience and determination, coupled with exceptional medical care, defied these expectations. His rehabilitation was extensive, involving months of physiotherapy, speech therapy, and psychological support to help him come to terms with the traumatic event and the profound grief of losing his mother and grandmother. The call from Dr Duffy was a poignant reminder of how close he came to joining them. She told him that his survival was nothing short of miraculous, a testament to the life-saving work done in those critical moments at the crash site near Carlisle. Logan, now a vocal advocate for the Great North Air Ambulance, often reflects on that day, acknowledging that without their rapid response, he would not be here today to share his story or remember his beloved Hayley Murdoch and Sheila Dixon. The scars, both physical and emotional, remain, but so does an immense gratitude for the second chance at life he received.

" I thought par would be a decent score on my first attempt , " a delighted Manley told BBC Radio Wales . Manley finished strongly with and eagle three on the par five 17th and a superb birdie four on the par-four 18th, completing a remarkable two-under-par round of 68. The Welshman, a relative unknown on the professional circuit and making his major championship debut, was visibly thrilled as he walked off the final green, acknowledging the cheers from the appreciative Royal Birkdale crowd. His impressive display, particularly his back-nine surge which saw him card three birdies and that crucial eagle, defied pre-tournament expectations in the notoriously challenging conditions.

Speaking further to BBC Radio Wales after his round, Manley reflected on the unexpected nature of his performance. "Honestly, I was just hoping to make the cut," he admitted with a grin. "To be up there on the leaderboard, even for a short while, is beyond anything I could have imagined. I've dreamt of playing in The Open my whole life, and to perform like this on the first day, at such an iconic venue like Royal Birkdale, it's just surreal. The course was brutal out there today with the wind and the rain coming in at times, so to post a score like that feels incredibly special."

His unexpected charge caught the attention of both seasoned golf commentators and the wider media. Suddenly, the focus wasn't just on the established stars, but on the plucky debutant who had briefly stolen the show. Manley’s humble demeanor and evident joy resonated with fans, who were quickly drawn to his underdog story. With three more rounds to play, the challenge of maintaining such form remained, but for one glorious day, the 38-year-old Welshman had announced his arrival on golf's biggest stage, setting a high bar for his own expectations and providing a compelling narrative for the championship.

Pearson said it was in discussions regarding the sale of the Economist but there was " no certainty that this process will lead to a transaction ". This divestment of its print media holdings, including the iconic Financial Times, signals a clear strategic pivot for Pearson. The company, under CEO John Fallon, is increasingly focusing on its global education business, aiming to streamline its portfolio and concentrate resources on digital learning and assessment tools. This marks the end of an era for Pearson as a diversified media conglomerate, aligning with a broader industry trend of specialization.

The potential sale of its 50% stake in the Economist Group, which publishes the influential weekly magazine, presents a more intricate challenge. Unlike the straightforward acquisition of the Financial Times by Japan's Nikkei, the Economist has a unique ownership structure designed to safeguard its editorial independence. A trust holds a significant portion of shares, and a consortium of long-standing family shareholders – including the Rothschilds, Cadburys, and Schroders, alongside Italy's powerful Agnelli family through their investment vehicle Exor – own the remaining stakes. John Elkann, chairman of Exor, had publicly expressed interest in increasing their shareholding, emphasizing their commitment to maintaining the publication's journalistic integrity and distinct ethos.

This inherent complexity, requiring consensus among existing shareholders deeply invested in the Economist's long-term vision, explains Pearson's cautious statement regarding "no certainty." For Pearson, completing these divestitures would solidify its identity as a pure-play education company, allowing it to dedicate all efforts to developing digital learning platforms globally and capitalize on the evolving education sector. These moves underscore the significant redefinition underway in the media and publishing industries.

For the first time, MPs have agreed in a vote that we will begin the process of leaving the EU by the end of March.
The government chief whip was seen with a massive grin after tonight's vote.
Remember ministers' climbdown came with a clever kicker, persuading Labour to sign up to their timetable for triggering Article 50 without committing to very much in return - the vague promise of a plan that could be as detailed as the back of the proverbial fag packet.
There's grumpiness on the Labour benches at how it was handled - angry conversations taking place, sources suggest - a sense among some that the front bench allowed themselves to be hoodwinked by the government's cunning plan.
Potential Tory rebels on the Remain side are deeply suspicious of the government's real intentions for giving more information about its ideas for Brexit. They backed off today, but will be back for more, no question.
But beyond the immediate machinations and the chief whip's big grin, two realities are confirmed by the events of the last 24 hours.
Yes - the numbers tonight suggest not very many MPs will actually try to block Brexit, or frustrate the process. They will certainly try to push the government for more details. They will certainly try to amend the proposals that eventually make it to the Commons, whenever that is. That could disrupt and delay things, but trying to stop it happening is not on the agenda of the vast majority.
But what's equally clear is that Theresa May does not have a secure majority on the EU. As soon as her plans (eventually) hit the floor of the House, she's likely to have to compromise.
That is precisely why the government is fighting so hard just across the road in the Supreme Court to try to avoid MPs having a say before the really hard work in Brussels even begins.

It was announced on Wednesday that the East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre , at Glenfield Hospital , was to stop children 's surgery services . It was one of 10 units under review nationally with the intention to focus expertise in fewer locations . The charity Heartlink said it would not accept the judgement . A spokesman for the charity , John Rigby , said : " We 're going to take stock , listen to what our reps have said, and then we will plan our next steps. This is absolutely not the end of the fight for the East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre. We believe this decision is flawed and will ultimately harm children and families across the UK. Heartlink will explore every avenue, including legal challenges and further campaigning, to reverse this damaging judgement."

This decision, part of NHS England's 'Safe and Sustainable' review, aims to consolidate specialist services into fewer, larger centres to improve outcomes for children with complex congenital heart conditions. While proponents cite better surgical results and comprehensive care through concentrated expertise, opponents like Heartlink argue that closing established units, especially those with strong reputations, fragments care and increases travel burden for families in regions like the East Midlands.

Glenfield Hospital's children's heart unit is also uniquely known for its Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) service, a vital life support system for failing hearts and lungs. It is one of only four paediatric ECMO centres in the UK. Though the ECMO service wasn't explicitly part of the surgical closure, clinicians and parents worry about the long-term viability of a specialist ECMO unit without a co-located surgical team. This interdependency is a core argument for campaigners like John Rigby, who fear that dismantling the surgical component will inevitably weaken or lead to the loss of the ECMO service, a crucial national resource. The future of specialist paediatric care in the UK is now under intense scrutiny, with questions raised about whether centralisation truly benefits all.

The Investigatory Powers Act gained royal assent in November . The government has said it will defend the act . Powers covered by the act allow state agencies to control and alter electronic devices , read texts , online messages and emails, monitor phone calls and access location data. This controversial legislation, dubbed the 'Snooper's Charter' by critics, grants extensive surveillance capabilities to agencies like MI5, MI6, and GCHQ. Liberty, with director Martha Spurrier at the forefront, argues the act constitutes an "assault on our freedom" by enabling mass surveillance. Spurrier contends it permits indiscriminate data collection on ordinary citizens, setting a dangerous precedent for civil liberties rather than targeting specific threats. She calls it one of the most extreme surveillance laws in a democracy. Despite significant opposition, including from the House of Lords which sought stronger privacy protections, the Investigatory Powers Act gained royal assent. The government, under then-Prime Minister Theresa May, defended the act as vital for national security in the digital age. May argued it merely updated existing powers, bringing transparency and proper oversight through independent judicial commissioners. However, Liberty and other privacy advocates continue to challenge its proportionality. They highlight concerns over bulk data collection, device hacking, and the requirement for internet service providers to retain browsing history for 12 months, viewing these as unacceptable intrusions. Legal challenges are anticipated, potentially reaching the European Court of Human Rights. The act underscores a fundamental tension between state security and individual freedoms, with critics warning of a chilling effect on free expression.

" The Hungarian Mate came into the contest with an impressive record with 17 wins in his 22 previous fights , but it was evident from the first bell that Mate was in for a tough night. Taylor, known for his explosive power and intelligent boxing, wasted no time in asserting his dominance. He moved fluidly, cutting off the ring and landing sharp, accurate jabs that quickly reddened Mate’s face. The Edinburgh crowd, already buzzing with anticipation, roared with every connection. Taylor’s southpaw stance and powerful left hand proved particularly problematic for the Hungarian, who struggled to find his rhythm or land anything significant in return.

Within the first minute, a blistering combination from Taylor – a left hook followed by a straight right – sent Mate stumbling backward into the ropes. The Commonwealth gold medallist, sensing an early finish, pressed home his advantage with relentless aggression. Mate showed commendable resilience, trying to clinch and weather the storm, but Taylor's precision and volume of punches were overwhelming. Just past the midway point of the opening round, a perfectly timed left uppercut from Taylor snapped Mate’s head back, followed by a crunching right hook that sent the visitor to the canvas.

The referee immediately began his count as Mate struggled to regain his footing, his eyes glazed. Although he managed to clamber upright at the count of nine, his legs were clearly unsteady, and the referee wisely waved off the contest, deeming him unable to continue. The official time of the stoppage was just 2 minutes and 10 seconds of the first round, a truly emphatic and devastating performance from the Prestonpans pugilist. The packed Meadowbank Arena erupted in a deafening roar, a standing ovation for their hometown hero.

After the fight, a beaming Taylor soaked in the adulation of the crowd, acknowledging their support. Speaking to BBC Scotland later, he reflected on the win, reiterating his surprise at the swiftness of the victory. "I came here expecting a tough fight, maybe a few rounds to get warmed up, but I caught him clean early and just went for it. The support from the fans was incredible, it really spurred me on."

Manager Barry McGuigan, the legendary former world champion, watched on with immense satisfaction. "Josh showed tonight exactly why we believe he's destined for greatness," McGuigan told reporters. "His power, his speed, his ring intelligence – it's all there. He handled the pressure of fighting at Meadowbank in front of his home fans perfectly. This was a statement win, a clear message to the super-lightweight division. We're not rushing anything, as I said before, we've got to take the right fights at the right time to develop him properly. But he's learning and improving with every bout. We'll sit down, review this performance, and plan the next step. There are big fights out there for Josh, and he’s ready for the challenges that lie ahead. This performance only confirms that he is truly a very special talent, someone who could go all the way to the top of the sport." The victory marked another significant milestone in Taylor's rapidly ascending professional career, setting the stage for even bigger challenges and proving his pedigree on home soil against a credible opponent, even if the fight itself didn't last long. Mencap chief executive Mark Goldring said: "We fear that unless the government commits to a strong action plan to close large institutions and develop appropriate local services for people with a learning disability, there is a very real risk that another Winterbourne View will come to light."

A Department of Health spokeswoman said: "We are clear that wherever possible people should be supported to live in their own homes within their local community.
"In a small number of cases people might need access to good quality assessment and treatment services which might include some short periods of in-patient care.

"It is vital all services are commissioned properly, reviewed regularly and not used as a long-term solution."

Writing in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing , clinicians say there is a growing trend for under-25s to seek the wrinkle - smoothing injections . But the research suggests " frozen faces " could stop young people from learning how to express emotions fully . A leading body of UK plastic surgeons says injecting teenagers for cosmetic reasons is " morally wrong " . Botox and other versions of the toxin work by temporarily paralysing muscles in the upper face to reduce wrinkling when people frown . Nurse practitioner Helen Collier , who carried out the research , says reality TV and social media are significant drivers behind this worrying trend. She observed that many young clients are influenced by the flawless, often filter-enhanced, appearances portrayed online and in popular culture, leading to unrealistic expectations about their own looks. Ms Collier, whose findings are detailed in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, expressed particular concern about the psychological implications of intervening with a developing brain's ability to express and interpret emotions. She explained that the muscles targeted by Botox are crucial not only for frowning but also for conveying a wide range of human emotions, from surprise to sadness. If these muscles are routinely paralysed from an early age, it could hinder a young person's capacity to fully experience and communicate their feelings, potentially impacting their social development and emotional intelligence.

The research highlighted that while older patients often seek Botox to reverse visible signs of aging, younger individuals are increasingly opting for "preventative Botox," hoping to stop wrinkles from forming in the first place. This shift in motivation raises profound ethical questions for practitioners. Ms Collier argues that genuine informed consent is difficult to obtain from teenagers, whose brains are still developing, and who may not fully grasp the long-term consequences of such procedures. She emphasized that the decision to undergo a cosmetic procedure like Botox should be made maturely, weighing the risks and benefits, something many under-25s are not yet equipped to do.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), a leading body of UK plastic surgeons, has echoed these concerns, reiterating its strong stance against cosmetic injections for those under 18, deeming it "morally wrong." Even for those slightly older but still under 25, BAAPS advises extreme caution and thorough psychological assessment before any treatment. They advocate for a focus on mental well-being and body positivity rather than promoting interventions that can have irreversible impacts on a young person's self-perception and emotional development.

Ms Collier's research, published in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing, urges clinicians to prioritize the mental health and developmental needs of young patients. She calls for stricter regulations around the marketing and administration of cosmetic injectables to minors and young adults, suggesting that a mandatory cooling-off period and psychological evaluation should be standard practice. She believes that practitioners have a duty of care to protect vulnerable individuals from potential harm, and this includes resisting the commercial pressures to provide treatments that may not be in the patient's best interest. The findings underscore the urgent need for a societal shift away from the relentless pursuit of an artificial ideal of perfection towards embracing natural beauty and promoting healthy self-esteem among young people in the UK and globally. This involves educating both practitioners and the public about the true purpose and potential downsides of procedures like Botox, ensuring that informed decisions are made, and that the emotional and psychological well-being of young people remains paramount. The long-term effects of widespread Botox use in this age group on collective emotional literacy and non-verbal communication are yet unknown, adding another layer of concern for experts like Helen Collier.

The study tracked more than 200,000 Australian smokers and non - smokers above the age of 45 over six years . Mortality risk went up with cigarette use , BMC Medicine reports . Smoking 10 cigarettes a day doubled the risk , while 20 - a - day smokers were four to five times more likely to die . Although someone who smokes could lead a long life , their habit makes this less likely . Smoking increases the risk of a multitude of health problems, including various cancers, cardiovascular diseases, and respiratory illnesses. The study, published in BMC Medicine, underscored the profound impact of even moderate smoking on mortality rates, reinforcing decades of research on the dangers of tobacco. Lung cancer is perhaps the most well-known consequence, but smoking also significantly elevates the risk of cancers of the throat, mouth, oesophagus, bladder, kidney, pancreas, stomach, and cervix, as well as acute myeloid leukaemia. Beyond cancer, smokers are at a much higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, and bronchitis. It also contributes to conditions like type 2 diabetes, age-related macular degeneration (leading to blindness), and osteoporosis, weakening bones.

Prof Emily Banks, a leading researcher involved in the BMC Medicine study, emphasised that "Even smoking a few cigarettes a day has substantial effects on mortality." Her work, along with findings from other major health organisations, consistently points to a clear dose-response relationship between cigarette use and adverse health outcomes. Organizations such as Cancer Research UK and the American Cancer Society have long championed public health campaigns to reduce smoking rates, highlighting the preventable nature of many tobacco-related diseases. In the UK, significant progress has been made in reducing smoking prevalence, but it remains a leading cause of premature death and illness. The message from health experts is clear: quitting smoking at any age can dramatically improve health prospects and extend life, reducing the heightened risks associated with continued tobacco use. Even for long-term smokers, quitting starts a process of healing and risk reduction that can add years to one's life and improve overall quality of health. The evidence is overwhelming: every cigarette takes a toll on the body, making the decision to quit one of the most beneficial steps an individual can take for their health and well-being.

A total of 374 employees lost their jobs when Tullis Russell Papermakers , based at Markinch in Fife , went into administration in April 2015 . Each employee received the equivalent of eight weeks ' wages in compensation for their loss . The award follows a judgement from an employment tribunal in Dundee, handed down earlier this year. The tribunal's decision found that Tullis Russell Papermakers, a company with a rich history stretching back over 200 years in Markinch, Fife, had failed to properly consult its employees and their union representatives on the mass redundancies before the company's collapse. This failure to adhere to the statutory obligation for collective consultation under the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, meant that workers were entitled to a protective award.

The case was spearheaded by former employees who sought justice for the abrupt and devastating job losses. David Martyn, a partner and specialist in employment law at the Dundee office of the law firm Gilson Gray LLP (formerly part of Bond Pearce, which was acquired), played a pivotal role in representing the affected workers. Martyn welcomed the tribunal’s finding, stating that it offered some measure of vindication and financial relief to the hundreds of individuals and families severely impacted by the mill's closure. He highlighted the importance of employers, even those facing insolvency, upholding their legal duties towards their workforce during redundancy processes.

The closure of Tullis Russell, a cornerstone of industry in Markinch and the wider Fife region, sent shockwaves through the community, marking the end of an era for papermaking in the area and leaving a significant void in the local economy. For the 374 employees, many of whom had dedicated decades of their working lives to the mill, the compensation, although limited to eight weeks' pay, provided essential support during a period of immense uncertainty and hardship. This protective award serves as a critical reminder of workers' rights during such challenging corporate transitions, ensuring that even in administration, companies are held accountable for their legal obligations concerning workforce redundancy.

Stefan Appleton , 18 , was with friends when he was attacked in Nightingale Park in Islington on 10 June last year . The killer stabbed him with the 25 in ( 63 cm ) serrated blade after leaping off a stolen moped , the Old Bailey heard . The 17 - year - old , who can not be named due to his age , was cleared of murder . He will be sentenced on 21 April . Mr Appleton , a popular and bright teenager, was an avid football fan and a beloved son and brother. His death sent shockwaves through the Islington community, leaving his family and friends devastated. He was described by those who knew him as a joyful and kind-hearted individual with a promising future ahead of him. The brutal nature of the attack, carried out in a public park, deeply rattled local residents and intensified concerns about knife crime among young people.

The Metropolitan Police launched a comprehensive investigation, meticulously gathering evidence and tracking down the perpetrator. Detectives worked tirelessly to piece together the events leading up to the fatal stabbing. The court heard how the assailant, riding a stolen moped, had pursued Stefan before cornering him in Nightingale Park, close to the area often referred to as the Red Pitch, a popular local recreation spot. The ferocity of the attack, involving a large serrated blade, was a key focus of the prosecution’s case.

During the trial at the Old Bailey, the prosecution argued that the defendant had demonstrated a clear intent to cause serious harm, if not death. However, the defence presented arguments challenging the specific intent required for a murder conviction, leading to the jury’s decision to clear the 17-year-old of murder, finding him guilty of manslaughter instead. This verdict, while acknowledging the defendant’s responsibility for Stefan’s death, has been met with mixed emotions by Stefan’s family, who had campaigned tirelessly for justice. They issued a statement expressing their profound grief and the permanent void left by Stefan’s passing, but also reiterated their commitment to advocating for an end to knife violence.

The sentencing hearing on 21 April will determine the consequences for the teenager who took Stefan’s life. The case has highlighted the urgent need for interventions to prevent similar tragedies and to address the root causes of youth violence in London. Stefan Appleton’s legacy, though tragically cut short, continues to serve as a poignant reminder of the devastating impact of knife crime on individuals, families, and communities like Islington.

The fine print of the deal suggests something slightly different , and shows that GM has in fact taken a hit of up to ¬£6bn in order to get shot of Vauxhall and Opel . First , a big chunk of the price - three - quarters of a billion pounds - is not for car plants , but for loans taken out by the owners of Opel and Vauxhall This unusual arrangement highlights that rather than simply selling an asset, GM is effectively paying to divest itself of a long-standing financial burden. The bulk of the £6bn charge, however, stems from the substantial pension liabilities that GM has chosen to retain rather than offload to Peugeot. Estimates place GM's retention of pension obligations for Vauxhall and Opel employees at well over £5bn, reflecting the enormous cost of legacy commitments built up over decades. This decision, made in Detroit, underscores GM's strategic imperative to clear its balance sheet of European losses that have plagued its financial performance for years. By retaining these liabilities, GM avoids the potentially complex and protracted negotiations that would have been required to transfer them to Peugeot, thereby expediting the sale and providing a clean break.

The deal, therefore, is less about GM selling a profitable division and more about a costly exit from a market where it has struggled to compete consistently. For Peugeot, this acquisition of Vauxhall and Opel presents an opportunity to significantly increase its market share in Europe and achieve substantial economies of scale. However, it also means inheriting a business that has been unprofitable for nearly two decades, requiring significant restructuring and investment to turn around. The challenge for Peugeot will be to integrate the Vauxhall and Opel operations efficiently, streamline production, and reduce costs without alienating the workforce or diluting the brands' appeal. The focus for Vauxhall under its new ownership will be on platform sharing with Peugeot models, standardizing components, and rationalizing the product portfolio to improve profitability. This move signals a definitive shift in GM's global strategy, allowing it to concentrate resources on more lucrative markets like North America and China, and invest heavily in future technologies such as electric and autonomous vehicles. The severance of ties with Vauxhall and Opel frees up capital and management attention, enabling GM to pursue its growth ambitions elsewhere, even if the price of freedom came with a hefty £6bn cheque.

The Arsenal FC midfielder , 24 , uploaded a picture from his 2014 wedding with the caption " un flwyddyn heddiw " , which means " one year [ ago ] today " . In contrast to positive responses , some users expressed confusion while others ridiculed the message . One questioned whether the FA Cup winner was " drunk " The confusion stemmed from a misunderstanding of the Welsh phrase "un flwyddyn heddiw." While perfectly natural and idiomatic Welsh for marking an anniversary – meaning "one year today" – many English-speaking social media users interpreted it literally, failing to grasp its linguistic nuance. Aaron Ramsey, a proud Welshman, had posted the picture from his 2014 wedding on what was clearly his first anniversary in 2015. However, some users assumed the caption meant the picture itself was exactly one year old, which made no sense for a 2014 wedding photo. Others simply couldn't reconcile a 2014 event with a "one year today" caption, leading them to believe the FA Cup winner was confused about his own wedding date.

The decision by Mr. Ramsey to use his native tongue, a common practice for the midfielder, was widely misinterpreted. One Twitter user, @rightjudgeiam, sarcastically tweeted, "Does Aaron Ramsey not know how long a year is? 2014 wedding, posts 'one year today'. Welsh or not, that's just bad maths." This reaction highlighted a lack of understanding regarding the traditional use of such anniversary greetings in Welsh culture. The ridicule often stemmed from assumptions that he was implying the 2014 wedding had only happened "one year today" relative to the 2015 post. This episode underscored the pitfalls of social media, where context, linguistic differences, and cultural nuances are easily lost, turning an innocent, culturally specific message into a subject of online amusement and mockery.

Ms Cristea , 31 , who was on holiday with boyfriend Andrei Burnaz , had been in hospital since the attack . It has emerged that Mr Burnaz had been planning to propose during the day out . A family statement confirmed Ms Cristea , who was an architect , had died on Thursday . The architect, who had been visiting London from Romania, was thrown into the River Thames during the rampage by Khalid Masood. She was rescued from the water but had suffered catastrophic head injuries and a severe lung infection, remaining in critical condition for weeks at St Thomas' Hospital. Her family, including her parents and sister, had maintained a constant vigil at her bedside, desperately hoping for her recovery, until her tragic passing.

Mr Burnaz, who sustained a fractured foot in the attack and has since undergone surgery, has spoken emotionally about the terrifying moments after they were hit and his desperate search for Andreea amidst the chaos. He described seeing Ms Cristea disappear into the water after being struck by the vehicle, and his frantic efforts to locate her before she was pulled out by rescuers. The couple, originally from Constanța, Romania, were on a romantic trip, and the revelation that Mr Burnaz had intended to propose adds a profoundly tragic layer to their story, highlighting the dreams and future abruptly stolen by the act of terror.

Ms Cristea's death tragically brings the total number of fatalities directly resulting from Khalid Masood's attack to five. The other victims were US tourist Kurt Cochran, retired window cleaner Leslie Rhodes, and mother-of-two Aysha Frade, all of whom were struck on Westminster Bridge, along with PC Keith Palmer, the brave officer stabbed to death by Masood at the gates of the Palace of Westminster. The attack, which stunned the world, transformed a bustling London landmark into a scene of unimaginable horror and grief.

Tributes have poured in for Andreea, remembering her as a vibrant, talented architect with a promising future. The Romanian Ambassador to the UK expressed deep sorrow, conveying the shared grief of the Romanian community for her loss. Her tragic passing is a stark reminder of the global reach of such violence, impacting individuals from diverse backgrounds who were simply enjoying a day out in a major capital. The investigation into Masood’s motives and potential associates continues, but the devastating human cost of his actions, epitomized by Ms Cristea and Mr Burnaz, remains the most poignant legacy. The Rhodesian Squadron Royal Air Force plane , based at RAF Wittering , crashed at Holme on 22 November 1940 . Pilot Officer Harold Penketh , from Brighton , did not bail out and died . The Spitfire remains were found after a geophysical survey of the area . It is hoped the recovered parts will be put on public display , offering a poignant reminder of the sacrifices made during World War Two.

Pilot Officer Penketh, aged just 20 at the time of the tragedy, was flying a Supermarine Spitfire Mk IIa, a crucial fighter aircraft during the Battle of Britain and its aftermath. While the exact cause of the crash remains unknown, it is speculated that he may have been attempting to steer his damaged aircraft away from the village of Holme, thus preventing further casualties on the ground, a common act of heroism among pilots of that era. His decision not to bail out, despite the clear danger, underscores the immense courage displayed by so many young men in the face of conflict. Harold Penketh's name is commemorated on the Brighton & Hove War Memorial, serving as a permanent tribute to his ultimate sacrifice.

The archaeological team, working closely with aviation historians and military experts, undertook a meticulous excavation following the successful geophysical survey. This state-of-the-art technique had revealed anomalies beneath the surface, consistent with buried metallic objects, leading them directly to the crash site. Over several weeks, a variety of artefacts were carefully unearthed, including fragments of the Spitfire's engine, sections of the fuselage, instrumentation, and personal effects believed to belong to Pilot Officer Penketh. Each piece recovered tells a part of the story, shedding light on the intensity of aerial combat and the grim reality faced by those defending the nation's skies.

The ongoing conservation efforts aim to stabilise and preserve these precious relics. Plans are underway to create an exhibit, potentially at a local museum or a dedicated aviation heritage centre, which will not only showcase the recovered Spitfire components but also tell the personal story of Harold Penketh and the wider context of the Rhodesian Squadron Royal Air Force's operations from RAF Wittering during the war. This display will serve as an educational resource, ensuring that the bravery of individuals like Penketh and the vital role of the Spitfire in Britain's defence are never forgotten. It will allow visitors to connect directly with a piece of history, understanding the profound human cost of freedom and the legacy of the young pilots who flew from bases like RAF Wittering. The community of Brighton, in particular, has expressed a deep interest in honouring one of their own through this significant historical recovery and memorial. The ultimate goal is to provide a fitting and lasting tribute to Pilot Officer Harold Penketh and all who served.

It should have been an easy try , but the Wales international , known for his relentless defensive work and never-say-die attitude, launched himself forward with a desperate lunge. The stadium, filled with passionate Italian fans roaring for Treviso, held its breath as Williams, defying the odds, somehow managed to get a hand to Senioli's ankle just inches from the try-line. The Treviso player stumbled, his momentum broken, and the ball, which he had been cradling loosely in anticipation of the score, was dislodged. It bounced once, tantalisingly close to the whitewash, before a Scarlets forward, arriving belatedly but opportunistically, dived on it, securing the turnover. The collective groan from the Italian crowd was almost as loud as the roar of relief from the small contingent of travelling Welsh supporters. Senioli, still sprawled on the turf, looked up in disbelief, the earlier smile replaced by a grimace of frustration. Scott Williams, quickly back on his feet, simply nodded, a silent testament to the high stakes of this cross-border encounter. This single moment, a testament to Williams's grit, shifted the momentum. Treviso, who had been dominating, suddenly looked rattled, while Scarlets, buoyed by the miraculous defensive stop, found a new surge of energy. The game, critical for both sides' European aspirations, hung finely in the balance, a true showcase of the intensity of rugby between Italy and Wales.

"It would do everything you asked of it. Compared to other aircraft it was light on the controls, you could do all the aerobatics and you would come up to speed very quickly.
"If you treated a Spitfire properly, it treated you properly. Treat it roughly or be careless with it and you were in trouble, in that it would do all sorts of things such as ground looping. It also had a very fragile undercarriage and could collapse."
Mr Costain was a member of the RAF for 37 years.

"There aren't many of us left [alive] that have flown the number of different marks of Spitfire that I have."
During and since his flying days, Mr Costain says he has often been asked if he was frightened during the war years.
He said: "I was terrified, but I was terrified of letting my own friends see that I was frightened. One made one's self very determined that you wouldn't show that.
"If you were attacked when you were flying a Spitfire during the war years, you turned hard into the attacking aircraft and they just couldn't get behind you! It was much more manoeuvrable than the German aircraft.
"I don't think we should ever forget what the Spitfire did for England. It was virtually England's saving grace."

Friday 's bomb hit a group of youth activists planning to cross into Syria to help rebuild the town of Kobane . A video shows the group holding a news conference to discuss their plans , when an explosion rips through the crowd. The chaotic footage, widely circulated online, shows bodies strewn across the ground, thick smoke billowing upwards, and survivors screaming amidst the debris. At least 32 people were killed in the attack in Suruc, a town bordering Syria, and over 100 were wounded. The vast majority of the victims were members of the Federation of Socialist Youth Associations (SGDF), who had gathered at the Amara Culture Centre before their planned journey to Kobane. Their mission was to help reconstruct the Syrian Kurdish town, which had been devastated by a four-month siege by Islamic State militants last year before being liberated by Kurdish forces.

The Turkish authorities swiftly identified the perpetrator as a female suicide bomber with suspected links to the Islamic State group, also known as ISIS or Daesh. This attack marked a significant escalation of the conflict onto Turkish soil, putting immense pressure on President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s government. Critics had long accused Ankara of turning a blind eye to, or even tacitly supporting, hardline Islamist groups in Syria as part of its strategy to undermine President Bashar al-Assad. However, following the Suruc bombing, Turkey vowed a more aggressive stance. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu condemned the 'barbaric' act and pledged to intensify efforts against all terrorist organizations.

The blast immediately ignited widespread outrage and protests across Turkey, especially in Istanbul, where demonstrators clashed violently with police. The previously mentioned use of water cannon, teargas, and rubber bullets underscores the ferocity of these confrontations, as protesters accused the government of complicity or negligence in failing to prevent such an attack. Many felt the bombing was a direct consequence of Turkey's perceived inaction against Islamic State, particularly along its lengthy border with Syria, which has been a conduit for foreign fighters joining militant groups.

In the days that followed, Turkish security forces launched a series of nationwide raids, detaining hundreds of suspected militants from various groups, including alleged members of the Islamic State. The government stated that these operations were a comprehensive crackdown on terrorism, moving beyond just ISIS to target Kurdish separatist groups like the PKK as well. This broader approach, however, drew criticism from those who believed it was an attempt to deflect attention from the core issue of Islamic State infiltration and to suppress Kurdish political movements. The bombing in Suruc profoundly reshaped Turkey’s domestic security landscape and its foreign policy towards Syria, signalling a more direct and assertive, albeit complex, engagement in the fight against regional extremism.

The impasse poses a significant challenge for the future of cricket between the two nations.
